pass1.sentence: Heat exhaustion is overheating that usually eases with cooling and rest, while heatstroke is an emergency for which the NHS says to call 999.
pass1.note: NHS summary: heatstroke emergency, dial 999; heat exhaustion managed by cooling, if no improvement after 30 minutes call 999

pass1.sentence: Heat exhaustion can cause tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling or being sick, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin and cramps.
Heatstroke is the more serious stage, with very hot skin that is not sweating, confusion, fast breathing, a fit or loss of consciousness.
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving somewhere cool, removing extra clothing, drinking water and cooling the skin.
The NHS says to call 999 if someone has not started to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, or if heatstroke is suspected.
Older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions are described as most vulnerable in hot weather.
Heat exhaustion happens when the body struggles to cope with heat.
Heatstroke is the more serious form, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.
The two are linked: NHS-linked sources say that heat exhaustion which does not improve after 30 minutes may be heatstroke.
pass1.note: search summaries: if no improvement after 30 minutes may have heatstroke

pass1.sentence: Heat exhaustion is generally not serious if the person cools down within that time.
pass1.note: summary: generally manageable if cooled within 30 minutes

pass1.sentence: The NHS lists tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling sick or being sick, and heavy sweating.
The skin can become pale and clammy, and there can be cramps and a high temperature.
In children, NHS-linked pages mention that they may become floppy and sleepy.
pass1.note: children summary: may become floppy and sleepy (NHS-linked local pages; Red Cross children page returned)

pass1.sentence: For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving the person somewhere cool and taking off unnecessary clothing.
It also describes giving plenty of water, or an isotonic sports drink or rehydration powder.
The skin can be cooled by spraying or sponging with cool water and fanning.
Cold packs wrapped in a cloth, placed under the armpits or on the neck, are also described.
The NHS says to stay with the person until they are better.
pass1.note: Stay with them until they're better

pass1.sentence: The NHS lists a very high temperature, and hot skin that is not sweating, among the warning signs of heatstroke.
Others are fast breathing, a fast heartbeat, confusion, restlessness, a seizure (fit) and loss of consciousness.
The NHS notes that redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.
pass1.note: red skin harder to spot on brown or black skin

pass1.sentence: If heatstroke is suspected, the NHS says to dial 999.
It also says not to drive to A&E.
pass1.note: Do not drive yourself to A&E

pass1.sentence: The NHS also says to call 999 if someone with heat exhaustion has not begun to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place.
The NHS describes cooling the person while waiting for the ambulance.
This can mean wrapping them in a cool, wet sheet, fanning them, or sponging them with cold water.
pass1.note: wrap in cool wet sheet / fan / sponge

pass1.sentence: If the person loses consciousness, the NHS describes putting them in the recovery position and telling the ambulance service.
pass1.note: recovery position and tell ambulance service

pass1.sentence: First-aid guidance on this site gives the same order: cooling and help first.
pass1.note: site first-aid.json: call 999, cool, recovery position if unresponsive

pass1.sentence: GOV.UK and NHS inform describe older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions as more vulnerable in hot weather.
pass1.note: higher-risk groups; babies and young children less able to regulate temperature (NHS inform)

pass1.sentence: Conditions named include heart, breathing and kidney problems and diabetes.
pass1.note: search summary: guidance commonly names these

pass1.sentence: Some medicines can affect sweating and temperature control, and NHS inform advises continuing prescribed medicines unless a health professional says otherwise.
pass1.note: search summary: continue medicines unless advised; some drugs affect sweating (one source)

pass1.sentence: For staying cool, the guidance describes closing curtains or blinds on rooms facing the sun, and opening windows at night when it is cooler outside.
It also describes planning activity for early morning or evening, drinking plenty of fluids, and limiting alcohol.
Never leave babies, children, older people or pets alone in a parked car, the guidance says.
pass1.note: never leave in a parked car

pass1.sentence: Checking on vulnerable neighbours, friends and relatives is also advised.
For an emergency, such as suspected heatstroke, the NHS says to call 999.
For worry about symptoms that are worsening but not an emergency, the NHS advice returned says to contact NHS 111.
pass1.note: If you are concerned... contact NHS 111

pass1.sentence: One NHS-linked source says that anyone worried about their health during a heatwave can contact a doctor, a pharmacist or NHS 111.
pass1.note: search summary: contacting doctor, pharmacist or NHS 111 wise if worried
